signs__RENAL / UROLOGICAL__Haematuria.front: What is the first step when a patient has a positive urine dipstick for blood?
signs__RENAL / UROLOGICAL__Haematuria.back: Confirm red cells on microscopy. A positive dipstick with no red cells means myoglobinuria (rhabdomyolysis) or haemoglobinuria (haemolysis), not true haematuria.

signs__RENAL / UROLOGICAL__Haematuria.front: What is the key rule for painless visible haematuria in an adult?
signs__RENAL / UROLOGICAL__Haematuria.back: It is a urological cancer (bladder / renal / upper-tract) until proven otherwise — refer on a 2-week-wait pathway for flexible cystoscopy and CT urogram.

signs__RENAL / UROLOGICAL__Haematuria.front: How do you tell a glomerular from a urological source of haematuria?
signs__RENAL / UROLOGICAL__Haematuria.back: Glomerular: dysmorphic red cells, red-cell casts, proteinuria, hypertension, AKI. Urological: clots, colic, an isolated bleed with timing in the stream and normal renal function.
Haematuria + proteinuria + hypertension + a rising creatinine (AKI), often with red-cell casts and dysmorphic red cells — a nephrology emergency (rapidly progressive GN can lose kidneys in days).

signs__RENAL / UROLOGICAL__Haematuria.front: What does the timing of blood within the urinary stream suggest?
signs__RENAL / UROLOGICAL__Haematuria.back: Initial haematuria = urethral; terminal = bladder base / prostate; total (throughout) = bladder or upper tract.

signs__RENAL / UROLOGICAL__Haematuria.front: What are the main risk factors for urothelial (bladder) cancer?
signs__RENAL / UROLOGICAL__Haematuria.back: Age ≥45, smoking, occupational aromatic amines / dyes, prior pelvic radiotherapy and cyclophosphamide.

signs__RENAL / UROLOGICAL__Haematuria.front: Which causes of haematuria are painful?
signs__RENAL / UROLOGICAL__Haematuria.back: Stones (colicky loin-to-groin pain), infection (dysuria / cystitis, or fever + loin pain in pyelonephritis) and clot retention; painless visible haematuria points to cancer.

signs__RENAL / UROLOGICAL__Haematuria.front: What is synpharyngitic haematuria and what does it suggest?
signs__RENAL / UROLOGICAL__Haematuria.back: Visible haematuria appearing 1–2 days after a sore throat / URTI; it suggests IgA nephropathy (in contrast to the ~2-week latency of post-streptococcal GN).

signs__RENAL / UROLOGICAL__Haematuria.front: Which investigations are used to work up haematuria?
signs__RENAL / UROLOGICAL__Haematuria.back: Urine microscopy (red-cell morphology, casts) + MSU culture + ACR/PCR; U&E/eGFR, FBC, clotting, BP; CT urogram + flexible cystoscopy; nephrology bloods (ANCA, anti-GBM, complement) and renal biopsy if glomerular.

signs__RENAL / UROLOGICAL__Haematuria.front: Which serological tests are sent when a glomerulonephritis or vasculitis is suspected?
signs__RENAL / UROLOGICAL__Haematuria.back: ANCA (vasculitis), anti-GBM (Goodpasture), complement (C3/C4), ANA/anti-dsDNA, and immunoglobulins — alongside urgent nephrology referral.
Schistosomiasis (Schistosoma haematobium) — classically terminal haematuria after freshwater exposure in an endemic area; a risk factor for bladder squamous cell carcinoma.

signs__RENAL / UROLOGICAL__Haematuria.front: Why should you not attribute haematuria to anticoagulation alone?
signs__RENAL / UROLOGICAL__Haematuria.back: Anticoagulation unmasks underlying pathology — a lesion (tumour, stone) must still be excluded with the standard haematuria work-up.

signs__RENAL / UROLOGICAL__Loin Pain.front: How is loin pain first triaged?
signs__RENAL / UROLOGICAL__Loin Pain.back: Into renal / urological (renal-angle tenderness, haematuria / dysuria, fever) vs referred (musculoskeletal spine, herpes zoster, basal pneumonia / pleurisy, biliary / bowel).

signs__RENAL / UROLOGICAL__Loin Pain.front: What loin-pain pattern indicates a ureteric stone?
signs__RENAL / UROLOGICAL__Loin Pain.back: Colicky loin-to-groin pain in a patient who cannot lie still, often with haematuria — covered in the Loin-to-Groin Pain topic.

signs__RENAL / UROLOGICAL__Loin Pain.front: What is the emergency of fever + loin pain + an obstructing stone?
signs__RENAL / UROLOGICAL__Loin Pain.back: An infected obstructed system (pyonephrosis) — pus under pressure. It needs emergency decompression (nephrostomy or ureteric stent) plus antibiotics and resuscitation, as sepsis develops rapidly.

signs__RENAL / UROLOGICAL__Loin Pain.front: Which vascular emergency mimics renal colic?
signs__RENAL / UROLOGICAL__Loin Pain.back: A leaking / ruptured abdominal aortic aneurysm — sudden flank / back pain + collapse or hypotension + a pulsatile mass in an older arteriopath. Never diagnose a first “renal colic” over 60 without excluding it.

signs__RENAL / UROLOGICAL__Loin Pain.front: What renal / urological causes give constant (non-colicky) loin pain?
signs__RENAL / UROLOGICAL__Loin Pain.back: Pyelonephritis, renal / perinephric abscess, obstruction / hydronephrosis, renal cell carcinoma, polycystic kidneys (bleed / infection), and renal infarction / vein thrombosis.

signs__RENAL / UROLOGICAL__Loin Pain.front: What does bilateral loin pain suggest?
signs__RENAL / UROLOGICAL__Loin Pain.back: Bilateral obstruction, polycystic kidney disease, or medical renal disease — and bilateral (or solitary-kidney) obstruction causes AKI / anuria.

signs__RENAL / UROLOGICAL__Loin Pain.front: Which features point to a musculoskeletal cause of loin pain?
signs__RENAL / UROLOGICAL__Loin Pain.back: Movement-related pain with tender paraspinal muscles and no urinary features or fever.

signs__RENAL / UROLOGICAL__Loin Pain.front: How does herpes zoster present in the loin?
signs__RENAL / UROLOGICAL__Loin Pain.back: A dermatomal band of pain (often before the rash), followed by a vesicular rash in the same dermatome — unilateral and not crossing the midline.

signs__RENAL / UROLOGICAL__Loin Pain.front: Which investigations are used for loin pain?
signs__RENAL / UROLOGICAL__Loin Pain.back: Urine dipstick + MSU culture; U&E / eGFR, FBC / CRP, blood cultures if febrile; CT KUB (stone / obstruction), ultrasound (hydronephrosis), contrast CT for abscess / infarction, and CT angiogram if an AAA is possible.

signs__RENAL / UROLOGICAL__Loin Pain.front: What predisposes to renal infarction or renal vein thrombosis?
signs__RENAL / UROLOGICAL__Loin Pain.back: Atrial fibrillation and other embolic sources (infarction); nephrotic syndrome and thrombophilia (renal vein thrombosis).

signs__RENAL / UROLOGICAL__Loin Pain.front: Why must a first episode of "renal colic" in an older patient be treated with caution?
signs__RENAL / UROLOGICAL__Loin Pain.back: Because a leaking AAA can present identically — a first stone over ~60, especially with hypotension or a pulsatile mass, must be imaged to exclude an aneurysm before accepting colic.

signs__RENAL / UROLOGICAL__Loin Pain.front: What is the management principle for an infected, obstructed kidney?
signs__RENAL / UROLOGICAL__Loin Pain.back: Decompress and treat: urgent nephrostomy or stent to relieve the obstruction, plus antibiotics and resuscitation — antibiotics alone are insufficient while pus is obstructed.

signs__RENAL / UROLOGICAL__Loin-to-Groin.front: What is the classic cause of loin-to-groin pain?
signs__RENAL / UROLOGICAL__Loin-to-Groin.back: Ureteric colic from a stone passing down the ureter — sudden, severe, colicky pain radiating from the loin to the groin (and scrotum / labia), with a characteristically restless, writhing patient.

signs__RENAL / UROLOGICAL__Loin-to-Groin.front: How does the behaviour of a patient with ureteric colic differ from one with peritonitis?
signs__RENAL / UROLOGICAL__Loin-to-Groin.back: Colic patients are restless and cannot lie still; peritonitis patients lie motionless because movement worsens the pain.

signs__RENAL / UROLOGICAL__Loin-to-Groin.front: What is the gold-standard investigation for a suspected ureteric stone?
signs__RENAL / UROLOGICAL__Loin-to-Groin.back: A non-contrast CT KUB. Ultrasound is used in pregnancy and younger patients to limit radiation.

signs__RENAL / UROLOGICAL__Loin-to-Groin.front: What is the great mimic of renal colic in an older patient?
signs__RENAL / UROLOGICAL__Loin-to-Groin.back: A leaking / ruptured abdominal aortic aneurysm — a first "renal colic" over 60, or colic with hypotension or a pulsatile mass, must have the aorta imaged (CT angiogram) before a stone is accepted.

signs__RENAL / UROLOGICAL__Loin-to-Groin.front: What must always be excluded in a woman of reproductive age with loin-to-groin / iliac-fossa pain?
signs__RENAL / UROLOGICAL__Loin-to-Groin.back: An ectopic pregnancy — always do a pregnancy test.

signs__RENAL / UROLOGICAL__Loin-to-Groin.front: What is the emergency of fever plus an obstructing stone?
signs__RENAL / UROLOGICAL__Loin-to-Groin.back: An infected obstructed system (pyonephrosis) — it needs emergency decompression (nephrostomy / stent) plus antibiotics; antibiotics alone are insufficient.

signs__RENAL / UROLOGICAL__Loin-to-Groin.front: At which sites does a ureteric stone commonly lodge?
signs__RENAL / UROLOGICAL__Loin-to-Groin.back: The three narrowings: the pelvi-ureteric junction (PUJ), the pelvic brim (crossing the iliac vessels), and the vesicoureteric junction (VUJ) — the VUJ is the commonest, and adds bladder irritability.

signs__RENAL / UROLOGICAL__Loin-to-Groin.front: What is the commonest type of urinary stone, and which type is radiolucent on X-ray?
signs__RENAL / UROLOGICAL__Loin-to-Groin.back: Calcium oxalate is commonest. Uric acid stones are radiolucent on plain X-ray (but still seen on CT) and are associated with high urate / gout.

signs__RENAL / UROLOGICAL__Loin-to-Groin.front: Which stone forms staghorn calculi and is associated with infection?
signs__RENAL / UROLOGICAL__Loin-to-Groin.back: Struvite (magnesium ammonium phosphate) stones, associated with urease-producing organisms (e.g. Proteus) and recurrent UTIs.

signs__RENAL / UROLOGICAL__Loin-to-Groin.front: How does stone size guide management?
signs__RENAL / UROLOGICAL__Loin-to-Groin.back: Stones <5 mm usually pass spontaneously (analgesia ± medical expulsive therapy); stones >10 mm rarely pass and usually need intervention (ureteroscopy, ESWL or PCNL).

signs__RENAL / UROLOGICAL__Loin-to-Groin.front: What is first-line analgesia for renal colic?
signs__RENAL / UROLOGICAL__Loin-to-Groin.back: NSAIDs (e.g. PR diclofenac) are first-line, with opioids if needed, plus an antiemetic and fluids.

signs__RENAL / UROLOGICAL__Loin-to-Groin.front: What is medical expulsive therapy for a ureteric stone?
signs__RENAL / UROLOGICAL__Loin-to-Groin.back: An alpha-blocker (e.g. tamsulosin) to relax the distal ureter and help passage of small distal (VUJ) stones.

signs__RENAL / UROLOGICAL__Loin-to-Groin.front: What follow-up is important after a stone episode?
signs__RENAL / UROLOGICAL__Loin-to-Groin.back: A metabolic work-up (serum calcium, urate, stone analysis) and prevention — hydration, dietary advice, and agents such as thiazides, allopurinol or citrate depending on stone type.

signs__RENAL / UROLOGICAL__Dysuria.front: What is the internal-vs-external split in dysuria?
signs__RENAL / UROLOGICAL__Dysuria.back: Internal dysuria (felt inside, throughout voiding) points to the bladder / urethra (cystitis, urethritis); external dysuria (stinging as urine passes over the vulva) points to a vulvovaginal cause.

signs__RENAL / UROLOGICAL__Dysuria.front: What is the commonest cause of dysuria and its typical features?
signs__RENAL / UROLOGICAL__Dysuria.back: Bacterial cystitis (UTI), especially in women: frequency, urgency, suprapubic pain and cloudy/offensive urine, with dipstick nitrites and leucocytes (usually E. coli).

signs__RENAL / UROLOGICAL__Dysuria.front: Which features indicate pyelonephritis rather than simple cystitis?
signs__RENAL / UROLOGICAL__Dysuria.back: Fever, loin pain and rigors (systemic upset) — upper-tract infection needing treatment and possible admission.

signs__RENAL / UROLOGICAL__Dysuria.front: How does acute bacterial prostatitis present?
signs__RENAL / UROLOGICAL__Dysuria.back: A man with fever, perineal / pelvic pain, LUTS and a tender, boggy prostate; there is a risk of urinary retention, and it needs a prolonged antibiotic course.

signs__RENAL / UROLOGICAL__Dysuria.front: Which STIs cause urethritis and dysuria, and how are they diagnosed?
signs__RENAL / UROLOGICAL__Dysuria.back: Chlamydia (commonest), gonorrhoea and Mycoplasma genitalium; diagnosed by NAAT, with treatment and partner notification.

signs__RENAL / UROLOGICAL__Dysuria.front: What distinguishes a UTI from urethritis/vaginitis as a cause of dysuria?
signs__RENAL / UROLOGICAL__Dysuria.back: UTI: frequency, urgency, suprapubic pain, positive nitrites/leucocytes. Urethritis: urethral discharge and sexual risk. Vaginitis: vaginal discharge/itch and external dysuria.

signs__RENAL / UROLOGICAL__Dysuria.front: When should a urine culture (MSU) be sent rather than treating on dipstick alone?
signs__RENAL / UROLOGICAL__Dysuria.back: In men, pregnancy, children, complicated or recurrent infections, and after treatment failure. A dipstick may suffice in an otherwise healthy non-pregnant woman.
Only in pregnancy (to prevent pyelonephritis and complications) — not routinely in the elderly, where it is common and over-treatment causes harm.
UTI in a man, pregnant woman or child, or with a catheter, structural / functional abnormality, recurrent infection or immunocompromise — these need culture and often investigation.

signs__RENAL / UROLOGICAL__Dysuria.front: What causes external dysuria in a postmenopausal woman?
signs__RENAL / UROLOGICAL__Dysuria.back: Atrophic vaginitis (oestrogen deficiency causing vulvovaginal dryness and irritation), managed with topical oestrogen.

signs__RENAL / UROLOGICAL__Dysuria.front: Which cause of dysuria must be excluded when there is also visible haematuria in an older smoker?
signs__RENAL / UROLOGICAL__Dysuria.back: Bladder cancer — arrange a haematuria work-up (flexible cystoscopy and CT urogram).

signs__RENAL / UROLOGICAL__Dysuria.front: What is the first-line antibiotic for uncomplicated cystitis in a non-pregnant woman?

signs__RENAL / UROLOGICAL__Lower Urinary.front: How are lower urinary tract symptoms (LUTS) classified?
signs__RENAL / UROLOGICAL__Lower Urinary.back: Into storage (irritative) — frequency, urgency, nocturia, urgency incontinence — and voiding (obstructive) — hesitancy, weak/intermittent stream, straining, terminal dribbling, incomplete emptying — plus post-micturition dribble.

signs__RENAL / UROLOGICAL__Lower Urinary.front: Why does the storage-vs-voiding split matter?
signs__RENAL / UROLOGICAL__Lower Urinary.back: It targets the cause and treatment: voiding LUTS in an older man is usually BPH / outlet obstruction (alpha-blocker, 5-ARI), while storage LUTS suggests an overactive bladder (antimuscarinic / mirabegron).

signs__RENAL / UROLOGICAL__Lower Urinary.front: What DRE findings distinguish BPH from prostate cancer?
signs__RENAL / UROLOGICAL__Lower Urinary.back: BPH: a smooth, symmetrically enlarged prostate. Prostate cancer: a hard, irregular / nodular prostate (with possible bone pain and a raised PSA).

signs__RENAL / UROLOGICAL__Lower Urinary.front: What red flags must be screened for in every patient with LUTS?
signs__RENAL / UROLOGICAL__Lower Urinary.back: Visible haematuria (bladder / prostate cancer), urinary retention (acute or chronic), a hard nodular prostate (cancer), and a neurological cause (e.g. cauda equina).

signs__RENAL / UROLOGICAL__Lower Urinary.front: What is high-pressure chronic retention and why is it dangerous?
signs__RENAL / UROLOGICAL__Lower Urinary.back: Painless chronic retention with a high post-void residual, overflow incontinence and a rising creatinine — it causes obstructive uropathy / renal failure and needs decompression.

signs__RENAL / UROLOGICAL__Lower Urinary.front: How does cauda equina present in the context of LUTS?
signs__RENAL / UROLOGICAL__Lower Urinary.back: LUTS (often retention) with saddle anaesthesia, bilateral leg symptoms and faecal incontinence / reduced anal tone — a surgical emergency needing an urgent MRI.

signs__RENAL / UROLOGICAL__Lower Urinary.front: Which investigations are used to assess LUTS?
signs__RENAL / UROLOGICAL__Lower Urinary.back: An IPSS symptom score and frequency-volume chart; DRE; urinalysis (infection, blood, glucose); U&E; PSA (after counselling); post-void residual (bladder scan); flow rate / urodynamics; ultrasound; and cystoscopy if haematuria.

signs__RENAL / UROLOGICAL__Lower Urinary.front: What are the main non-prostatic and systemic causes of LUTS?
signs__RENAL / UROLOGICAL__Lower Urinary.back: Overactive bladder, UTI, bladder stone, interstitial cystitis, neurogenic bladder (MS, spinal disease, Parkinson’s, diabetes), polyuria (diabetes / diabetes insipidus), diuretics, caffeine and constipation.

signs__RENAL / UROLOGICAL__Lower Urinary.front: What is the medical management of voiding LUTS due to BPH?
signs__RENAL / UROLOGICAL__Lower Urinary.back: An alpha-blocker (e.g. tamsulosin — rapid symptom relief) and, for a large prostate, a 5-alpha-reductase inhibitor (e.g. finasteride — shrinks it over months); TURP for refractory or complicated disease.

signs__RENAL / UROLOGICAL__Lower Urinary.front: What is the medical management of an overactive (storage) bladder?
signs__RENAL / UROLOGICAL__Lower Urinary.back: Conservative measures (fluid/caffeine reduction, bladder training) plus an antimuscarinic (e.g. solifenacin) or a beta-3 agonist (mirabegron).

signs__RENAL / UROLOGICAL__Lower Urinary.front: What must be excluded when LUTS is accompanied by visible haematuria?
signs__RENAL / UROLOGICAL__Lower Urinary.back: Bladder or prostate cancer — arrange flexible cystoscopy and CT urogram.

signs__RENAL / UROLOGICAL__Acute Urinary.back: The sudden, painful inability to pass urine with a palpable, tender, distended bladder (dull to percussion) — in contrast to painless chronic retention.

signs__RENAL / UROLOGICAL__Acute Urinary.front: What is the immediate management of acute urinary retention?
signs__RENAL / UROLOGICAL__Acute Urinary.back: Catheterise (urethral, or suprapubic if urethral fails) to relieve it, and record the residual volume drained — then find and treat the cause.

signs__RENAL / UROLOGICAL__Acute Urinary.front: What is the commonest cause of acute urinary retention?
signs__RENAL / UROLOGICAL__Acute Urinary.back: Benign prostatic hyperplasia in an older man, usually with a precipitant (constipation, a new drug, a UTI, alcohol or recent surgery).

signs__RENAL / UROLOGICAL__Acute Urinary.front: Which drugs commonly precipitate acute urinary retention?
signs__RENAL / UROLOGICAL__Acute Urinary.back: Anticholinergics, opioids, and sympathomimetics / decongestants (alpha-agonists) — and constipation and alcohol also contribute.

signs__RENAL / UROLOGICAL__Acute Urinary.front: How does cauda equina present in a patient with retention?
signs__RENAL / UROLOGICAL__Acute Urinary.back: Retention with saddle anaesthesia, bilateral leg symptoms, back pain and faecal incontinence / reduced anal tone — an emergency needing urgent MRI and surgery.

signs__RENAL / UROLOGICAL__Acute Urinary.front: What is post-obstructive diuresis and when does it occur?
signs__RENAL / UROLOGICAL__Acute Urinary.back: A large diuresis after decompressing high-pressure (obstructive) retention — monitor urine output and U&E and replace fluids to avoid dehydration and electrolyte disturbance.

signs__RENAL / UROLOGICAL__Acute Urinary.front: How is clot retention (from heavy haematuria) managed differently?
signs__RENAL / UROLOGICAL__Acute Urinary.back: It needs a 3-way catheter with bladder irrigation, not a standard catheter, to wash out clots.

signs__RENAL / UROLOGICAL__Acute Urinary.front: Why is a PSA unreliable in acute urinary retention?
signs__RENAL / UROLOGICAL__Acute Urinary.back: Retention (and catheterisation, UTI, DRE) falsely raises PSA, so it should be deferred until the acute episode has settled.

signs__RENAL / UROLOGICAL__Acute Urinary.front: What is the difference between acute and chronic urinary retention?
signs__RENAL / UROLOGICAL__Acute Urinary.back: Acute retention is painful with a moderately full bladder; chronic retention is painless, high-volume, and may present with overflow incontinence and renal impairment.

signs__RENAL / UROLOGICAL__Acute Urinary.front: What examination findings are important in acute retention?
signs__RENAL / UROLOGICAL__Acute Urinary.back: A palpable, tender, dull suprapubic bladder; a DRE (prostate size/consistency, faecal impaction, anal tone); and a focused neurological exam (saddle sensation, legs).

signs__RENAL / UROLOGICAL__Acute Urinary.front: After catheterisation for acute retention due to BPH, what is the ongoing plan?
signs__RENAL / UROLOGICAL__Acute Urinary.back: Treat the precipitant, start an alpha-blocker, and plan a trial without catheter (TWOC); if it fails, consider longer-term catheter or surgery (TURP) and urology referral.

signs__RENAL / UROLOGICAL__Chronic Urina.back: Painless, gradual, incomplete bladder emptying with a large post-void residual (often over a litre) — painless because the bladder stretches slowly (unlike acute retention).

signs__RENAL / UROLOGICAL__Chronic Urina.front: What is the key distinction within chronic urinary retention?
signs__RENAL / UROLOGICAL__Chronic Urina.back: Low-pressure (compliant bladder, normal kidneys) vs high-pressure (pressure transmitted to the upper tracts causing bilateral hydronephrosis, renal failure and nocturnal enuresis) — high-pressure is the dangerous form.

signs__RENAL / UROLOGICAL__Chronic Urina.front: What clinical clue suggests high-pressure chronic retention?
signs__RENAL / UROLOGICAL__Chronic Urina.back: Nocturnal enuresis (bed-wetting) in an adult, plus bilateral hydronephrosis and a raised creatinine.
A large diuresis after decompressing high-pressure retention — the patient can lose litres, so monitor urine output and U&E and replace fluids to prevent hypovolaemia and electrolyte disturbance.

signs__RENAL / UROLOGICAL__Chronic Urina.front: Why should you avoid a quick trial without catheter in high-pressure chronic retention?
signs__RENAL / UROLOGICAL__Chronic Urina.back: Because it frequently recurs and threatens the kidneys — it usually needs long-term drainage or definitive surgery rather than a rapid TWOC.

signs__RENAL / UROLOGICAL__Chronic Urina.front: How does chronic retention differ from acute retention?
signs__RENAL / UROLOGICAL__Chronic Urina.back: Chronic is painless, high-volume and gradual (often with overflow / enuresis); acute is painful with a tense, tender bladder.

signs__RENAL / UROLOGICAL__Chronic Urina.front: Why is overflow incontinence from a palpable bladder actually retention?
signs__RENAL / UROLOGICAL__Chronic Urina.back: The continuous dribbling occurs because the bladder is chronically full and over-distended — the treatment is to drain the bladder, not to treat it as a primary incontinence.

signs__RENAL / UROLOGICAL__Chronic Urina.front: What are the common causes of chronic urinary retention?
signs__RENAL / UROLOGICAL__Chronic Urina.back: BPH (commonest), prostate cancer, urethral stricture, and a neurogenic / atonic bladder (diabetes, MS, spinal-cord disease, Parkinson’s).

signs__RENAL / UROLOGICAL__Chronic Urina.front: Which investigations grade the pressure and assess the kidneys in chronic retention?
signs__RENAL / UROLOGICAL__Chronic Urina.back: A bladder scan (residual), U&E (renal function) and a renal-tract ultrasound (hydronephrosis, bladder-wall trabeculation); urodynamics if a neurogenic cause is suspected.

signs__RENAL / UROLOGICAL__Chronic Urina.front: What is the management of a neurogenic (atonic) bladder causing chronic retention?
signs__RENAL / UROLOGICAL__Chronic Urina.back: Intermittent (self-)catheterisation to empty the bladder regularly, alongside treating the underlying cause.

signs__RENAL / UROLOGICAL__Chronic Urina.front: What should be monitored after catheterising high-pressure chronic retention?
signs__RENAL / UROLOGICAL__Chronic Urina.back: Urine output and U&E for a post-obstructive diuresis, with fluid replacement; also watch for decompression haematuria.

signs__RENAL / UROLOGICAL__Urinary Incon.front: What are the main types of urinary incontinence?
signs__RENAL / UROLOGICAL__Urinary Incon.back: Stress (leak on effort), urgency (overactive bladder), mixed, overflow (chronic retention), continuous (fistula / ectopic ureter) and functional (cannot reach the toilet).

signs__RENAL / UROLOGICAL__Urinary Incon.front: What characterises stress urinary incontinence and its first-line treatment?
signs__RENAL / UROLOGICAL__Urinary Incon.back: Leakage on effort (cough, sneeze, exercise) from a weak sphincter / pelvic floor (childbirth, menopause, post-prostatectomy); first-line treatment is pelvic-floor muscle training.

signs__RENAL / UROLOGICAL__Urinary Incon.front: What characterises urgency incontinence and its management?
signs__RENAL / UROLOGICAL__Urinary Incon.back: A sudden urge followed by leakage, with frequency, urgency and nocturia, from detrusor overactivity (overactive bladder); managed with bladder training plus an antimuscarinic or mirabegron (botulinum toxin if refractory).

signs__RENAL / UROLOGICAL__Urinary Incon.front: What is overflow incontinence and how is it managed?
signs__RENAL / UROLOGICAL__Urinary Incon.back: Continuous dribbling from a chronically full bladder (chronic retention) — managed by relieving the retention (catheter / intermittent self-catheterisation, treating the obstruction), not with incontinence drugs.

signs__RENAL / UROLOGICAL__Urinary Incon.front: What does continuous leakage of urine suggest?
signs__RENAL / UROLOGICAL__Urinary Incon.back: A vesicovaginal fistula (after obstetric injury, pelvic surgery, radiotherapy or malignancy) or an ectopic ureter — needs investigation and surgical referral.
Leakage in someone with a normal urinary tract who cannot reach the toilet in time because of immobility, cognitive impairment or environmental barriers.

signs__RENAL / UROLOGICAL__Urinary Incon.front: What do the reversible causes of incontinence (DIPPERS) stand for?
Which investigations anchor the assessment of incontinence?
signs__RENAL / UROLOGICAL__Urinary Incon.back: A bladder diary (frequency-volume chart), urinalysis (infection, glucose, blood) and a post-void residual (to exclude overflow); urodynamics if the diagnosis is unclear or before surgery.

signs__RENAL / UROLOGICAL__Urinary Incon.front: Why is a post-void residual important in incontinence?
signs__RENAL / UROLOGICAL__Urinary Incon.back: It detects overflow incontinence due to chronic retention masquerading as incontinence — a high residual changes management entirely (treat the retention).

signs__RENAL / UROLOGICAL__Urinary Incon.front: What surgical options exist for stress incontinence?
signs__RENAL / UROLOGICAL__Urinary Incon.back: A mid-urethral sling or colposuspension in women, and an artificial urinary sphincter in men (e.g. post-prostatectomy); reserved after conservative measures.

signs__RENAL / UROLOGICAL__Urinary Incon.front: What red flags accompanying incontinence require urgent action?
signs__RENAL / UROLOGICAL__Urinary Incon.back: New incontinence with saddle anaesthesia / bilateral leg symptoms (cauda equina → MRI), continuous leakage (fistula), overflow from retention (renal impairment), and visible haematuria (cancer).

signs__RENAL / UROLOGICAL__Oliguria / An.front: How are oliguria and anuria defined?
How is the cause of oliguria/anuria (acute kidney injury) classified?
signs__RENAL / UROLOGICAL__Oliguria / An.back: Into pre-renal (hypoperfusion), renal/intrinsic (ATN, interstitial nephritis, glomerulonephritis, rhabdomyolysis) and post-renal (obstruction / blocked catheter).

signs__RENAL / UROLOGICAL__Oliguria / An.front: What is the commonest and first-checked cause of ward "anuria"?
signs__RENAL / UROLOGICAL__Oliguria / An.back: A blocked urinary catheter — always flush or replace it first before further investigation.

signs__RENAL / UROLOGICAL__Oliguria / An.front: Why does anuria specifically raise concern?
signs__RENAL / UROLOGICAL__Oliguria / An.back: Anuria strongly suggests obstruction (bilateral or of a single kidney), a blocked catheter, or a vascular catastrophe (bilateral renal artery/vein occlusion) — rather than typical pre-renal AKI.

signs__RENAL / UROLOGICAL__Oliguria / An.front: What are the features of pre-renal acute kidney injury?
signs__RENAL / UROLOGICAL__Oliguria / An.back: Hypoperfusion (hypovolaemia, sepsis, cardiac failure, hepatorenal) with concentrated urine and low urine sodium; the kidney is structurally intact and it responds to restored perfusion.

signs__RENAL / UROLOGICAL__Oliguria / An.front: What is the commonest intrinsic renal cause of AKI and its urinary finding?
signs__RENAL / UROLOGICAL__Oliguria / An.back: Acute tubular necrosis (from ischaemia or nephrotoxins), classically with muddy-brown granular casts on urine microscopy; it does not respond to fluids.

signs__RENAL / UROLOGICAL__Oliguria / An.front: What is the immediate life-threatening complication of AKI to treat?
signs__RENAL / UROLOGICAL__Oliguria / An.back: Hyperkalaemia — check an ECG (peaked T waves, broad QRS) and treat with calcium gluconate, insulin–dextrose and salbutamol.

signs__RENAL / UROLOGICAL__Oliguria / An.front: What are the AEIOU indications for urgent dialysis?
Which drugs are common nephrotoxins to stop in AKI?
signs__RENAL / UROLOGICAL__Oliguria / An.back: NSAIDs, ACE inhibitors / ARBs, aminoglycosides and iodinated contrast — and doses of renally-cleared drugs should be reviewed.

signs__RENAL / UROLOGICAL__Oliguria / An.front: How is post-renal (obstructive) AKI confirmed and managed?
signs__RENAL / UROLOGICAL__Oliguria / An.back: A bladder scan and renal ultrasound (hydronephrosis) confirm obstruction; management is to decompress (urethral catheter for outlet obstruction, nephrostomy for ureteric obstruction).

signs__RENAL / UROLOGICAL__Oliguria / An.front: Which urine test helps distinguish pre-renal AKI from acute tubular necrosis?
signs__RENAL / UROLOGICAL__Oliguria / An.back: Urine sodium / osmolality: pre-renal shows low urine sodium and concentrated urine; ATN shows higher urine sodium and an inability to concentrate.

signs__RENAL / UROLOGICAL__Haematuria.question: A 68-year-old smoker reports two episodes of passing frankly bloody urine with no pain. Renal function and urine microscopy show no casts. What is the most appropriate management?
options: 2-week-wait referral for cystoscopy and CT urogram
Reassure and repeat urine dip in 3 months
signs__RENAL / UROLOGICAL__Haematuria.explanation: Painless visible haematuria in an older smoker is a urological cancer until proven otherwise — urgent 2-week-wait cystoscopy + CT urogram.

signs__RENAL / UROLOGICAL__Haematuria.question: A urine dipstick is strongly positive for blood, but microscopy shows no red cells. The patient has muscle pain and dark urine after a collapse. What is the most likely explanation?
signs__RENAL / UROLOGICAL__Haematuria.explanation: A positive dip with no red cells on microscopy, plus muscle pain, indicates myoglobinuria (rhabdomyolysis), not true haematuria.

signs__RENAL / UROLOGICAL__Haematuria.question: A 25-year-old develops visible haematuria one day after a sore throat, with mild hypertension and protein on dipstick. What is the most likely diagnosis?
signs__RENAL / UROLOGICAL__Haematuria.explanation: Synpharyngitic haematuria (within 1–2 days of a URTI) with proteinuria/hypertension suggests IgA nephropathy; post-streptococcal GN typically follows ~2 weeks later.

signs__RENAL / UROLOGICAL__Haematuria.question: Which finding on urine microscopy points to a glomerular rather than urological source of bleeding?
signs__RENAL / UROLOGICAL__Haematuria.explanation: Red-cell casts (and dysmorphic red cells) indicate a glomerular source; clots indicate a urological source.

signs__RENAL / UROLOGICAL__Haematuria.question: A patient has haematuria, new hypertension, protein +++ on dipstick and a creatinine that has doubled in a week. What is the priority?
options: Urgent nephrology referral for suspected rapidly progressive glomerulonephritis
signs__RENAL / UROLOGICAL__Haematuria.explanation: This nephritic picture with rising creatinine may be a rapidly progressive GN / vasculitis and needs urgent nephrology — kidneys can be lost within days.

signs__RENAL / UROLOGICAL__Haematuria.question: A 30-year-old presents with sudden severe colicky pain radiating from the left loin to the groin, with visible haematuria. What is the most likely cause?
signs__RENAL / UROLOGICAL__Haematuria.explanation: Colicky loin-to-groin pain with haematuria is classic for a renal / ureteric stone; confirm with a non-contrast CT KUB.

signs__RENAL / UROLOGICAL__Haematuria.question: Which is the most important initial test to distinguish true haematuria from other causes of red urine?
signs__RENAL / UROLOGICAL__Haematuria.explanation: Urine microscopy confirms red cells (true haematuria) and can show casts/morphology, distinguishing it from myoglobin, haemoglobin, food and drugs.

signs__RENAL / UROLOGICAL__Haematuria.question: A returning traveller from sub-Saharan Africa has terminal haematuria after swimming in a freshwater lake. Which diagnosis should be considered?
signs__RENAL / UROLOGICAL__Haematuria.explanation: Schistosomiasis (S. haematobium) causes terminal haematuria after freshwater exposure and predisposes to bladder squamous cell carcinoma.

signs__RENAL / UROLOGICAL__Haematuria.question: Which imaging and endoscopic combination is used to investigate visible haematuria for a urological cause?
signs__RENAL / UROLOGICAL__Haematuria.explanation: Suspected urological-source haematuria is investigated with a CT urogram (upper tracts) and flexible cystoscopy (bladder).

signs__RENAL / UROLOGICAL__Haematuria.question: A patient on warfarin (INR in range) has visible haematuria. What is the correct approach?
options: Attribute it to the warfarin and reassure
Investigate as for any haematuria — anticoagulation unmasks pathology
Repeat the dip in 6 months only
signs__RENAL / UROLOGICAL__Haematuria.explanation: Anticoagulation unmasks underlying lesions; a full haematuria work-up is still required.

signs__RENAL / UROLOGICAL__Haematuria.question: An older man reports poor stream, hesitancy and terminal dribbling with intermittent haematuria. Besides BPH, what must be excluded?
signs__RENAL / UROLOGICAL__Haematuria.explanation: LUTS with haematuria may be BPH, but prostate or bladder cancer must be excluded before attributing bleeding to benign disease.

signs__RENAL / UROLOGICAL__Haematuria.question: What does terminal haematuria (blood at the end of the stream) most suggest?
options: A bladder base or prostatic source
signs__RENAL / UROLOGICAL__Haematuria.explanation: Terminal haematuria localises to the bladder base or prostate; initial haematuria is urethral and total haematuria is bladder/upper tract.

signs__RENAL / UROLOGICAL__Loin Pain.question: A 55-year-old has right loin pain, a fever of 39C with rigors, and dysuria. A CT shows an obstructing ureteric stone with hydronephrosis. What is the most appropriate management?
signs__RENAL / UROLOGICAL__Loin Pain.explanation: Fever + obstruction = an infected obstructed system (pyonephrosis), a urological emergency needing decompression plus antibiotics — antibiotics alone will not clear pus under pressure.

signs__RENAL / UROLOGICAL__Loin Pain.question: A 72-year-old smoker presents with sudden severe left flank pain radiating to the back, feeling faint, with a blood pressure of 90/60 and a pulsatile abdominal mass. What is the most likely diagnosis?
signs__RENAL / UROLOGICAL__Loin Pain.explanation: Sudden flank/back pain with collapse and a pulsatile mass in an older arteriopath is a leaking AAA until proven otherwise — not renal colic.

signs__RENAL / UROLOGICAL__Loin Pain.question: A 30-year-old has fever, rigors, right loin pain and dysuria; urine dip shows leucocytes, nitrites and blood. What is the most likely diagnosis?
signs__RENAL / UROLOGICAL__Loin Pain.explanation: Fever, rigors, loin pain and dysuria with an active urine dip indicate acute pyelonephritis; confirm with an MSU culture.

signs__RENAL / UROLOGICAL__Loin Pain.question: A patient with atrial fibrillation develops sudden severe loin pain with haematuria and a markedly raised LDH; urine culture is negative. What is the most likely diagnosis?
signs__RENAL / UROLOGICAL__Loin Pain.explanation: Sudden loin pain with haematuria and a raised LDH in a patient with AF (an embolic source) suggests renal infarction (a renal vascular event).

signs__RENAL / UROLOGICAL__Loin Pain.question: A 40-year-old with hypertension and a family history of kidney failure has bilateral loin discomfort and ballotable flank masses. What is the most likely diagnosis?
signs__RENAL / UROLOGICAL__Loin Pain.explanation: Bilateral loin discomfort with ballotable kidneys, hypertension and a family history indicates polycystic kidney disease.

signs__RENAL / UROLOGICAL__Loin Pain.question: Which feature best distinguishes musculoskeletal loin pain from renal pain?
options: Pain worse on movement with tender paraspinal muscles and no urinary features
signs__RENAL / UROLOGICAL__Loin Pain.explanation: Movement-related pain with paraspinal tenderness and no urinary features or fever points to a musculoskeletal cause.

signs__RENAL / UROLOGICAL__Loin Pain.question: A patient describes a band of severe unilateral loin pain for 3 days, and now a crop of vesicles has appeared in the same area. What is the diagnosis?
signs__RENAL / UROLOGICAL__Loin Pain.explanation: A dermatomal band of pain followed by vesicles is herpes zoster (shingles).

signs__RENAL / UROLOGICAL__Loin Pain.question: What is the most appropriate first-line imaging to identify a stone causing loin pain?
signs__RENAL / UROLOGICAL__Loin Pain.explanation: A non-contrast CT KUB is the first-line test for a suspected renal/ureteric stone and obstruction.

signs__RENAL / UROLOGICAL__Loin Pain.question: A patient has persistent fever and loin pain despite 48 hours of antibiotics for presumed pyelonephritis. What complication should be excluded?
signs__RENAL / UROLOGICAL__Loin Pain.explanation: Failure to improve on antibiotics should prompt a contrast CT to exclude a renal / perinephric abscess or an obstructed, infected system.

signs__RENAL / UROLOGICAL__Loin Pain.question: An older man is diagnosed with his first "renal colic". Which finding should prompt urgent CT angiography rather than a CT KUB?
options: Hypotension and a pulsatile abdominal mass
signs__RENAL / UROLOGICAL__Loin Pain.explanation: Hypotension and a pulsatile mass raise concern for a leaking AAA — image the aorta urgently rather than assume a stone.

signs__RENAL / UROLOGICAL__Loin Pain.question: Why is decompression essential (not just antibiotics) in an infected obstructed kidney?
options: Antibiotics cannot clear pus trapped behind an obstruction
signs__RENAL / UROLOGICAL__Loin Pain.explanation: Pus under pressure behind an obstruction will not clear with antibiotics alone — relieving the obstruction (nephrostomy/stent) is essential.

signs__RENAL / UROLOGICAL__Loin Pain.question: A patient has a loin mass, visible haematuria and unintentional weight loss. Which diagnosis must be excluded?
signs__RENAL / UROLOGICAL__Loin Pain.explanation: A loin mass with haematuria and weight loss is suspicious for renal cell carcinoma — investigate with a CT urogram.

signs__RENAL / UROLOGICAL__Loin-to-Groin.question: A 35-year-old man has sudden severe right-sided pain radiating from the flank to the groin. He is rolling around unable to get comfortable, and urine dip shows blood. What is the most likely diagnosis?
signs__RENAL / UROLOGICAL__Loin-to-Groin.explanation: Restless loin-to-groin colic with haematuria is classic ureteric colic from a stone; confirm with a non-contrast CT KUB.

signs__RENAL / UROLOGICAL__Loin-to-Groin.question: A 68-year-old smoker presents with his first episode of "renal colic", is hypotensive, and has a pulsatile abdominal mass. What is the most appropriate imaging?
signs__RENAL / UROLOGICAL__Loin-to-Groin.explanation: A first colic over 60 with hypotension and a pulsatile mass is a leaking AAA until excluded — image the aorta urgently, not just the renal tract.

signs__RENAL / UROLOGICAL__Loin-to-Groin.question: Which behavioural feature helps distinguish ureteric colic from peritonitis?
options: The patient is restless and cannot lie still
The patient prefers to sit forward
The patient walks with a limp
The patient cannot straighten the leg
signs__RENAL / UROLOGICAL__Loin-to-Groin.explanation: Colic makes patients restless and writhing; peritonitis makes them lie still.

signs__RENAL / UROLOGICAL__Loin-to-Groin.question: A woman of 28 presents with left iliac-fossa and groin pain. Before diagnosing renal colic, what is essential?
options: A pregnancy test to exclude ectopic pregnancy
signs__RENAL / UROLOGICAL__Loin-to-Groin.explanation: In a reproductive-age woman, a pregnancy test is essential to exclude an ectopic pregnancy.

signs__RENAL / UROLOGICAL__Loin-to-Groin.question: A patient with a known obstructing ureteric stone develops a fever of 39C and rigors. What is the priority?
options: Continue analgesia and await stone passage
signs__RENAL / UROLOGICAL__Loin-to-Groin.explanation: Fever with an obstructing stone = an infected obstructed system needing emergency decompression plus antibiotics.

signs__RENAL / UROLOGICAL__Loin-to-Groin.question: Which is the commonest site for a ureteric stone to lodge?
signs__RENAL / UROLOGICAL__Loin-to-Groin.explanation: The vesicoureteric junction is the narrowest point and the commonest place for a stone to lodge, causing bladder irritability.

signs__RENAL / UROLOGICAL__Loin-to-Groin.question: A stone is not seen on a plain KUB X-ray but is clearly visible on CT. The patient has a history of gout. What type of stone is most likely?
signs__RENAL / UROLOGICAL__Loin-to-Groin.explanation: Uric acid stones are radiolucent on plain X-ray (seen on CT) and are linked to high urate / gout.

signs__RENAL / UROLOGICAL__Loin-to-Groin.question: A 4 mm distal ureteric stone is confirmed in a stable, apyrexial patient. What is the most appropriate initial management?
signs__RENAL / UROLOGICAL__Loin-to-Groin.explanation: A small (<5 mm) distal stone usually passes with analgesia and an alpha-blocker (medical expulsive therapy).

signs__RENAL / UROLOGICAL__Loin-to-Groin.question: What is the recommended first-line analgesia for renal colic?
signs__RENAL / UROLOGICAL__Loin-to-Groin.explanation: NSAIDs are first-line for renal colic, with opioids as needed.

signs__RENAL / UROLOGICAL__Loin-to-Groin.question: A recurrent stone-former has a staghorn calculus and repeated Proteus urinary infections. What stone type is this?
signs__RENAL / UROLOGICAL__Loin-to-Groin.explanation: Struvite stones form staghorn calculi in the setting of urease-producing (e.g. Proteus) infections.

signs__RENAL / UROLOGICAL__Loin-to-Groin.question: A young man presents with sudden severe pain that he localises to the groin and scrotum, with a tender high-riding testis. What must be excluded?
signs__RENAL / UROLOGICAL__Loin-to-Groin.explanation: Acute scrotal pain with a high-riding, tender testis is testicular torsion — a time-critical diagnosis that can mimic or accompany groin pain.

signs__RENAL / UROLOGICAL__Loin-to-Groin.question: After a stone has passed, which follow-up is appropriate to reduce recurrence?
options: Metabolic work-up and preventive advice (hydration, diet, +/- medication)
signs__RENAL / UROLOGICAL__Loin-to-Groin.explanation: A metabolic work-up (calcium, urate, stone analysis) and prevention (hydration, diet, thiazide/allopurinol/citrate) reduce recurrence.

signs__RENAL / UROLOGICAL__Dysuria.question: A 24-year-old woman has dysuria, frequency, urgency and suprapubic discomfort with cloudy urine. She is otherwise well and not pregnant. What is the most appropriate management?
options: Send MSU and await culture before treating
signs__RENAL / UROLOGICAL__Dysuria.explanation: Uncomplicated cystitis in a healthy non-pregnant woman is treated empirically with a short course of nitrofurantoin (or trimethoprim).

signs__RENAL / UROLOGICAL__Dysuria.question: A 30-year-old man has dysuria for a week with a mucoid urethral discharge. What is the most appropriate investigation?
options: STI NAAT for chlamydia and gonorrhoea
signs__RENAL / UROLOGICAL__Dysuria.explanation: Dysuria with urethral discharge in a sexually active man is urethritis — test with a NAAT for chlamydia and gonorrhoea, and arrange partner notification.

signs__RENAL / UROLOGICAL__Dysuria.question: A 45-year-old woman has dysuria, fever of 39C, rigors and right loin pain. What is the most likely diagnosis?
signs__RENAL / UROLOGICAL__Dysuria.explanation: Fever, rigors and loin pain indicate pyelonephritis (upper-tract infection), not simple cystitis.

signs__RENAL / UROLOGICAL__Dysuria.question: A 55-year-old man has dysuria, fever, perineal pain and a tender, boggy prostate on gentle examination. What is the diagnosis?
signs__RENAL / UROLOGICAL__Dysuria.explanation: Fever with perineal pain and a tender boggy prostate in a man is acute bacterial prostatitis, requiring a prolonged antibiotic course.

signs__RENAL / UROLOGICAL__Dysuria.question: A pregnant woman is found to have asymptomatic bacteriuria on a routine MSU. What is the correct action?
options: Do not treat, as she is asymptomatic
Repeat the sample in the third trimester only
signs__RENAL / UROLOGICAL__Dysuria.explanation: Asymptomatic bacteriuria in pregnancy should be treated to prevent pyelonephritis and adverse outcomes.

signs__RENAL / UROLOGICAL__Dysuria.question: A 26-year-old woman has external dysuria, vulval itch and a thick white curdy discharge. What is the most likely diagnosis?
signs__RENAL / UROLOGICAL__Dysuria.explanation: Itch with a curdy white discharge and external dysuria is vulvovaginal candidiasis.

signs__RENAL / UROLOGICAL__Dysuria.question: Which patient with dysuria should always have a urine culture rather than empirical treatment on dipstick alone?
options: A healthy young non-pregnant woman with classic cystitis
A woman with a single previous UTI
A patient who prefers not to be cultured
signs__RENAL / UROLOGICAL__Dysuria.explanation: UTI in a man is complicated by definition — send a culture and investigate the underlying cause.

signs__RENAL / UROLOGICAL__Dysuria.question: A 70-year-old male smoker reports dysuria and has passed visibly bloody urine. What must be excluded?
signs__RENAL / UROLOGICAL__Dysuria.explanation: Dysuria with visible haematuria in an older smoker mandates a bladder-cancer work-up (cystoscopy + CT urogram).

signs__RENAL / UROLOGICAL__Dysuria.question: An 82-year-old nursing-home resident has bacteriuria on dipstick but no urinary symptoms and is systemically well. What is the appropriate approach?
options: Treat with a 7-day course of antibiotics
signs__RENAL / UROLOGICAL__Dysuria.explanation: Asymptomatic bacteriuria is common in the elderly and should not be treated (except in pregnancy); over-treatment causes harm.

signs__RENAL / UROLOGICAL__Dysuria.question: Which finding points to a vulvovaginal rather than urinary cause of dysuria?
options: External (stinging as urine passes over the vulva) dysuria with vaginal discharge
signs__RENAL / UROLOGICAL__Dysuria.explanation: External dysuria with vaginal discharge/itch indicates a vulvovaginal cause; internal dysuria with urinary features points to the urinary tract.

signs__RENAL / UROLOGICAL__Dysuria.question: A young man with dysuria is diagnosed with chlamydial urethritis. Besides antibiotics, what is essential?
signs__RENAL / UROLOGICAL__Dysuria.explanation: Partner notification (contact tracing) is essential in managing a sexually transmitted infection.

signs__RENAL / UROLOGICAL__Dysuria.question: Which organism most commonly causes uncomplicated bacterial cystitis?
signs__RENAL / UROLOGICAL__Dysuria.explanation: Escherichia coli is the commonest cause of uncomplicated cystitis.

signs__RENAL / UROLOGICAL__Lower Urinary.question: An 68-year-old man reports hesitancy, a weak intermittent stream, terminal dribbling and a sensation of incomplete emptying. On DRE the prostate is smoothly enlarged. What is the most likely diagnosis?
signs__RENAL / UROLOGICAL__Lower Urinary.explanation: Voiding LUTS with a smooth, enlarged prostate is typical of benign prostatic hyperplasia.

signs__RENAL / UROLOGICAL__Lower Urinary.question: A 55-year-old woman has urgency, frequency and nocturia with no dysuria and a negative urine dip. What class of LUTS and likely diagnosis is this?
options: Voiding symptoms due to outlet obstruction
Storage symptoms due to overactive bladder
signs__RENAL / UROLOGICAL__Lower Urinary.explanation: Urgency, frequency and nocturia are storage symptoms; with no infection they suggest an overactive bladder.

signs__RENAL / UROLOGICAL__Lower Urinary.question: A 70-year-old man with LUTS has a hard, irregular prostate on DRE and new lower back pain. What is the most important next step?
options: PSA, then MRI and prostate biopsy
signs__RENAL / UROLOGICAL__Lower Urinary.explanation: A hard, nodular prostate with bone pain suggests prostate cancer — investigate with PSA, MRI and biopsy.

signs__RENAL / UROLOGICAL__Lower Urinary.question: A man with longstanding LUTS is found to have a palpable non-tender bladder, overflow incontinence and a creatinine that has risen markedly. What is the diagnosis?
options: Urethral stricture with normal renal function
signs__RENAL / UROLOGICAL__Lower Urinary.explanation: A painless palpable bladder with overflow and rising creatinine is high-pressure chronic retention causing obstructive uropathy — it needs decompression.

signs__RENAL / UROLOGICAL__Lower Urinary.question: A patient with new LUTS also reports numbness around the perineum, weakness in both legs and faecal incontinence. What is the priority?
options: Urgent MRI to exclude cauda equina syndrome
signs__RENAL / UROLOGICAL__Lower Urinary.explanation: LUTS with saddle anaesthesia, bilateral leg weakness and faecal incontinence indicates cauda equina — an emergency needing urgent MRI.

signs__RENAL / UROLOGICAL__Lower Urinary.question: Which first-line drug provides rapid symptom relief for voiding LUTS due to BPH?
signs__RENAL / UROLOGICAL__Lower Urinary.explanation: An alpha-blocker relaxes prostatic smooth muscle and gives rapid relief; 5-ARIs shrink a large prostate but take months.

signs__RENAL / UROLOGICAL__Lower Urinary.question: A 72-year-old smoker with irritative LUTS passes visibly bloody urine. What must be excluded?
signs__RENAL / UROLOGICAL__Lower Urinary.explanation: Irritative LUTS with visible haematuria in a smoker requires a bladder-cancer work-up (cystoscopy + CT urogram).

signs__RENAL / UROLOGICAL__Lower Urinary.question: Which investigation best quantifies incomplete bladder emptying at the bedside?
signs__RENAL / UROLOGICAL__Lower Urinary.explanation: A post-void residual bladder scan measures the urine left after voiding, quantifying incomplete emptying.

signs__RENAL / UROLOGICAL__Lower Urinary.question: A patient with storage LUTS and no red flags has failed conservative measures. Which drug class is appropriate?
signs__RENAL / UROLOGICAL__Lower Urinary.explanation: Storage symptoms / overactive bladder are treated with an antimuscarinic or mirabegron.

signs__RENAL / UROLOGICAL__Lower Urinary.question: Which systemic condition should be considered when LUTS includes marked polyuria with thirst and weight loss?
signs__RENAL / UROLOGICAL__Lower Urinary.explanation: Marked polyuria with thirst and weight loss suggests diabetes mellitus (or diabetes insipidus) rather than a primary bladder cause.

signs__RENAL / UROLOGICAL__Lower Urinary.question: Before checking a PSA in a man with LUTS, what should be done?
options: Counsel the patient about the implications of the result
signs__RENAL / UROLOGICAL__Lower Urinary.explanation: PSA testing requires counselling about its limitations and implications; recent infection, DRE or ejaculation can also raise it.

signs__RENAL / UROLOGICAL__Lower Urinary.question: Which two bedside assessments are mandatory in the initial evaluation of LUTS?
signs__RENAL / UROLOGICAL__Lower Urinary.explanation: A DRE (prostate) and urinalysis (infection, blood, glucose) are mandatory first-line assessments.

signs__RENAL / UROLOGICAL__Acute Urinary.question: A 75-year-old man cannot pass urine for 8 hours and has severe suprapubic pain with a palpable, tender bladder. What is the immediate management?
options: Urethral catheterisation and record the residual volume
Oral alpha-blocker and review in a week
signs__RENAL / UROLOGICAL__Acute Urinary.explanation: Acute retention is relieved by immediate catheterisation, recording the drained residual volume, before investigating the cause.

signs__RENAL / UROLOGICAL__Acute Urinary.question: A man in acute urinary retention also reports numbness around the perineum, weakness in both legs and new faecal incontinence. What is the priority after catheterisation?
options: Urgent MRI to exclude cauda equina
signs__RENAL / UROLOGICAL__Acute Urinary.explanation: Retention with saddle anaesthesia, bilateral leg weakness and faecal incontinence indicates cauda equina — an emergency needing urgent MRI.

signs__RENAL / UROLOGICAL__Acute Urinary.question: After catheterising a man with high-pressure chronic-on-acute retention (creatinine raised, bilateral hydronephrosis), what must be monitored?
options: Urine output and U&E for post-obstructive diuresis
signs__RENAL / UROLOGICAL__Acute Urinary.explanation: Decompressing high-pressure retention can cause a post-obstructive diuresis — monitor urine output and U&E and replace fluids.

signs__RENAL / UROLOGICAL__Acute Urinary.question: Which medication class most commonly precipitates acute urinary retention?
signs__RENAL / UROLOGICAL__Acute Urinary.explanation: Anticholinergic drugs (along with opioids and decongestants) commonly precipitate acute retention.

signs__RENAL / UROLOGICAL__Acute Urinary.question: A man in acute retention is draining heavily blood-stained urine with clots via the catheter, which then blocks. What is the appropriate catheter?
signs__RENAL / UROLOGICAL__Acute Urinary.explanation: Clot retention requires a 3-way catheter with irrigation to clear clots and keep the catheter patent.

signs__RENAL / UROLOGICAL__Acute Urinary.question: Why should a PSA test be avoided during an episode of acute urinary retention?
options: Retention and catheterisation falsely raise the PSA
PSA is only useful in women
PSA cannot be measured with a catheter
signs__RENAL / UROLOGICAL__Acute Urinary.explanation: Acute retention, catheterisation, UTI and DRE all raise PSA, so the test should be deferred.

signs__RENAL / UROLOGICAL__Acute Urinary.question: What single feature best distinguishes acute from chronic urinary retention?
options: Chronic retention is always smaller volume
Acute retention never needs a catheter
Acute retention is painful; chronic is painless
Acute retention causes no bladder distension
signs__RENAL / UROLOGICAL__Acute Urinary.explanation: Acute retention is painful; chronic retention is painless and typically high-volume.

signs__RENAL / UROLOGICAL__Acute Urinary.question: A 70-year-old man in acute retention is found to have a hard, irregular prostate on DRE. What does this suggest?
signs__RENAL / UROLOGICAL__Acute Urinary.explanation: A hard, nodular prostate suggests prostate cancer (a smooth enlarged prostate suggests BPH); investigate with PSA/MRI/biopsy once settled.

signs__RENAL / UROLOGICAL__Acute Urinary.question: Following catheterisation for BPH-related acute retention, which medication is started to improve the chance of a successful trial without catheter?
signs__RENAL / UROLOGICAL__Acute Urinary.explanation: An alpha-blocker started before a trial without catheter improves the likelihood of successful voiding.

signs__RENAL / UROLOGICAL__Acute Urinary.question: What volume of urine drained on catheterisation typically confirms acute retention?
signs__RENAL / UROLOGICAL__Acute Urinary.explanation: Typically 500–1000 mL is drained, and relief of the pain confirms the diagnosis.

signs__RENAL / UROLOGICAL__Acute Urinary.question: Besides prostatic causes, which common precipitant should be actively sought and treated in acute retention?
signs__RENAL / UROLOGICAL__Acute Urinary.explanation: Constipation is a common, reversible precipitant of acute retention and should be treated.

signs__RENAL / UROLOGICAL__Acute Urinary.question: A woman develops acute urinary retention 12 hours after a normal vaginal delivery. What is the most likely explanation?
signs__RENAL / UROLOGICAL__Acute Urinary.explanation: Post-partum retention is a recognised transient cause; catheterise and it usually resolves.

signs__RENAL / UROLOGICAL__Chronic Urina.question: A 78-year-old man is found to have a hugely distended but painless bladder, dribbling incontinence and a creatinine of 320 with bilateral hydronephrosis on ultrasound. What is the diagnosis?
options: Low-pressure chronic retention with normal kidneys
signs__RENAL / UROLOGICAL__Chronic Urina.explanation: A painless distended bladder with hydronephrosis and renal impairment is high-pressure chronic retention — the dangerous form.

signs__RENAL / UROLOGICAL__Chronic Urina.question: After catheterising a patient with high-pressure chronic retention, 4 litres drain and urine output remains very high. What must be done?
options: Monitor U&E and urine output and replace fluids (post-obstructive diuresis)
signs__RENAL / UROLOGICAL__Chronic Urina.explanation: A post-obstructive diuresis can lose litres — monitor U&E and output and replace fluids to prevent hypovolaemia.

signs__RENAL / UROLOGICAL__Chronic Urina.question: Which feature distinguishes chronic from acute urinary retention?
options: Chronic retention always has a smaller residual
Chronic retention only occurs in women
signs__RENAL / UROLOGICAL__Chronic Urina.explanation: Chronic retention is painless and high-volume; acute retention is painful.

signs__RENAL / UROLOGICAL__Chronic Urina.question: An adult man reports new bed-wetting at night. Combined with a palpable bladder and a raised creatinine, what does this suggest?
signs__RENAL / UROLOGICAL__Chronic Urina.explanation: Nocturnal enuresis in an adult with a palpable bladder and renal impairment is a hallmark of high-pressure chronic retention.

signs__RENAL / UROLOGICAL__Chronic Urina.question: A patient has continuous urinary dribbling and a large palpable bladder. How is this best understood?
options: Overflow incontinence due to chronic retention
signs__RENAL / UROLOGICAL__Chronic Urina.explanation: Continuous dribbling from a chronically over-distended bladder is overflow incontinence due to retention — drain the bladder.

signs__RENAL / UROLOGICAL__Chronic Urina.question: Which investigation best distinguishes high-pressure from low-pressure chronic retention?
signs__RENAL / UROLOGICAL__Chronic Urina.explanation: Renal-tract ultrasound (hydronephrosis) and U&E determine whether the retention is high-pressure and threatening the kidneys.

signs__RENAL / UROLOGICAL__Chronic Urina.question: What is the most common cause of chronic urinary retention in men?
signs__RENAL / UROLOGICAL__Chronic Urina.explanation: Benign prostatic hyperplasia is the commonest cause of chronic retention in men.

signs__RENAL / UROLOGICAL__Chronic Urina.question: A diabetic patient with a large residual and an atonic bladder on urodynamics has chronic retention. What is the appropriate long-term management?
signs__RENAL / UROLOGICAL__Chronic Urina.explanation: A neurogenic / atonic bladder is best managed with intermittent self-catheterisation to empty the bladder regularly.

signs__RENAL / UROLOGICAL__Chronic Urina.question: Why is a rapid trial without catheter usually inappropriate in high-pressure chronic retention?
options: It commonly recurs and threatens the kidneys, needing definitive management
It is only used in women
signs__RENAL / UROLOGICAL__Chronic Urina.explanation: High-pressure retention typically recurs and endangers renal function, so long-term drainage or definitive surgery is preferred over a quick TWOC.

signs__RENAL / UROLOGICAL__Chronic Urina.question: What bladder finding is characteristic of chronic retention on examination?
options: A painless, palpable, dull suprapubic mass
signs__RENAL / UROLOGICAL__Chronic Urina.explanation: Chronic retention gives a painless, palpable, dull suprapubic bladder.

signs__RENAL / UROLOGICAL__Chronic Urina.question: A man with chronic retention has a hard, irregular prostate on DRE. What must be excluded?
signs__RENAL / UROLOGICAL__Chronic Urina.explanation: A hard, nodular prostate raises concern for prostate cancer — investigate with PSA, MRI and biopsy.

signs__RENAL / UROLOGICAL__Chronic Urina.question: Which complication of chronic obstruction should be actively screened for at diagnosis?
signs__RENAL / UROLOGICAL__Chronic Urina.explanation: Longstanding obstruction can cause obstructive uropathy and chronic kidney disease — check renal function and imaging.

signs__RENAL / UROLOGICAL__Urinary Incon.question: A 52-year-old woman leaks small amounts of urine when she coughs, sneezes or exercises, but has no urgency. What type of incontinence is this and what is first-line treatment?
signs__RENAL / UROLOGICAL__Urinary Incon.explanation: Leakage on effort without urgency is stress incontinence; pelvic-floor muscle training is first-line.

signs__RENAL / UROLOGICAL__Urinary Incon.question: A 60-year-old man has a sudden strong urge to void followed by leakage, with frequency and nocturia. What is the diagnosis?
signs__RENAL / UROLOGICAL__Urinary Incon.explanation: A sudden urge then leakage with frequency/nocturia is urgency incontinence from an overactive bladder.

signs__RENAL / UROLOGICAL__Urinary Incon.question: A frail man has continuous dribbling of urine and a palpable bladder; the post-void residual is 900 mL. What is the mechanism?
signs__RENAL / UROLOGICAL__Urinary Incon.explanation: A palpable bladder with a large residual indicates overflow incontinence due to chronic retention — treat the retention.

signs__RENAL / UROLOGICAL__Urinary Incon.question: A woman has constant, uncontrollable urinary leakage that began after a difficult hysterectomy. What is the most likely cause?
signs__RENAL / UROLOGICAL__Urinary Incon.explanation: Continuous leakage after pelvic surgery suggests a vesicovaginal fistula, requiring investigation and surgical repair.

signs__RENAL / UROLOGICAL__Urinary Incon.question: An 85-year-old with dementia and poor mobility wets herself because she cannot get to the toilet in time; her urinary tract is otherwise normal. What type of incontinence is this?
signs__RENAL / UROLOGICAL__Urinary Incon.explanation: Functional incontinence is leakage from an inability to reach the toilet despite a normal urinary tract.

signs__RENAL / UROLOGICAL__Urinary Incon.question: Which bedside test is most important to exclude overflow before treating incontinence?
signs__RENAL / UROLOGICAL__Urinary Incon.explanation: A post-void residual excludes overflow incontinence from retention, which would change management.

signs__RENAL / UROLOGICAL__Urinary Incon.question: First-line management of an overactive bladder after conservative measures fail includes which drug class?
signs__RENAL / UROLOGICAL__Urinary Incon.explanation: Overactive bladder / urgency incontinence is treated with an antimuscarinic or mirabegron after bladder training.

signs__RENAL / UROLOGICAL__Urinary Incon.question: The mnemonic DIPPERS is used to remember what in the context of incontinence?
signs__RENAL / UROLOGICAL__Urinary Incon.explanation: DIPPERS lists the reversible/transient causes (Delirium, Infection, atrophic vaginitis, Pharmaceuticals, Psychological, Endocrine, Restricted mobility, Stool impaction).

signs__RENAL / UROLOGICAL__Urinary Incon.question: A woman with both leakage on coughing and episodes of urge-related leakage is diagnosed with which type?
signs__RENAL / UROLOGICAL__Urinary Incon.explanation: Features of both stress and urgency indicate mixed incontinence.

signs__RENAL / UROLOGICAL__Urinary Incon.question: A patient develops new incontinence with numbness around the perineum and weakness in both legs. What is the priority?
options: Urgent MRI to exclude cauda equina
signs__RENAL / UROLOGICAL__Urinary Incon.explanation: New incontinence with saddle anaesthesia and bilateral leg weakness is cauda equina — an emergency needing urgent MRI.

signs__RENAL / UROLOGICAL__Urinary Incon.question: Which is the recommended surgical option for stress incontinence in a woman who has failed conservative treatment?
options: Artificial urinary sphincter as first choice
signs__RENAL / UROLOGICAL__Urinary Incon.explanation: A mid-urethral sling (or colposuspension) is used for stress incontinence after conservative measures fail.

signs__RENAL / UROLOGICAL__Urinary Incon.question: An older woman presents with new urinary incontinence, dysuria and cloudy urine. What should be done before further incontinence work-up?
options: Treat the urinary tract infection (a reversible cause)
signs__RENAL / UROLOGICAL__Urinary Incon.explanation: A UTI is a reversible (DIPPERS) cause — treat it before pursuing a full incontinence work-up.

signs__RENAL / UROLOGICAL__Oliguria / An.question: A ward patient with a urinary catheter suddenly stops draining urine and becomes anuric. What is the first action?
signs__RENAL / UROLOGICAL__Oliguria / An.explanation: A blocked catheter is the commonest cause of sudden ward anuria — flush or replace it first.

signs__RENAL / UROLOGICAL__Oliguria / An.question: An oliguric post-operative patient is hypotensive with dry mucous membranes; urine is concentrated with a low sodium. What is the most likely type of AKI?
signs__RENAL / UROLOGICAL__Oliguria / An.explanation: Hypovolaemia with concentrated, low-sodium urine indicates pre-renal AKI, which should respond to restored perfusion.

signs__RENAL / UROLOGICAL__Oliguria / An.question: An AKI patient has a potassium of 6.9 mmol/L with peaked T waves on ECG. What is the immediate priority?
signs__RENAL / UROLOGICAL__Oliguria / An.explanation: Hyperkalaemia with ECG changes needs IV calcium for cardiac protection, then insulin–dextrose and salbutamol to shift potassium.

signs__RENAL / UROLOGICAL__Oliguria / An.question: An oliguric patient has muddy-brown granular casts on urine microscopy and did not respond to a fluid challenge, following a period of hypotension. What is the diagnosis?
signs__RENAL / UROLOGICAL__Oliguria / An.explanation: Muddy-brown granular casts with no fluid response after ischaemia indicate acute tubular necrosis.

signs__RENAL / UROLOGICAL__Oliguria / An.question: An anuric patient is found to have a palpable bladder and bilateral hydronephrosis on ultrasound. What is the management?
signs__RENAL / UROLOGICAL__Oliguria / An.explanation: Post-renal obstruction is reversible — decompress with a catheter (outlet) or nephrostomy (ureteric).

signs__RENAL / UROLOGICAL__Oliguria / An.question: Which set of criteria indicates the need for urgent dialysis in AKI?
signs__RENAL / UROLOGICAL__Oliguria / An.explanation: The AEIOU criteria (refractory acidosis, hyperkalaemia, intoxication, fluid overload, uraemia) indicate urgent dialysis.

signs__RENAL / UROLOGICAL__Oliguria / An.question: A patient develops AKI with a rash, fever and eosinophilia two weeks after starting a new antibiotic. What is the most likely cause?
signs__RENAL / UROLOGICAL__Oliguria / An.explanation: A drug-related AKI with rash, fever and eosinophilia is typical of acute interstitial nephritis.

signs__RENAL / UROLOGICAL__Oliguria / An.question: Which combination of drugs is most nephrotoxic and should be stopped in AKI?
signs__RENAL / UROLOGICAL__Oliguria / An.explanation: The NSAID + ACE inhibitor (± diuretic) "triple whammy" is a classic nephrotoxic combination to stop in AKI.

signs__RENAL / UROLOGICAL__Oliguria / An.question: A patient with AKI after a prolonged period lying on the floor has a very high creatine kinase and dark urine. What is the mechanism?
signs__RENAL / UROLOGICAL__Oliguria / An.explanation: A raised CK with dark (myoglobin) urine after immobility indicates rhabdomyolysis causing AKI.

signs__RENAL / UROLOGICAL__Oliguria / An.question: Which bedside assessment most directly guides fluid management in oliguria?
options: Volume status (BP, JVP, mucous membranes, oedema)
signs__RENAL / UROLOGICAL__Oliguria / An.explanation: Assessing volume status determines whether the patient is fluid-deplete (pre-renal, give fluids) or overloaded (restrict / consider dialysis).

signs__RENAL / UROLOGICAL__Oliguria / An.question: An oliguric patient has blood and protein on dipstick with red-cell casts and hypertension. What category of AKI is this?
signs__RENAL / UROLOGICAL__Oliguria / An.explanation: Blood, protein and red-cell casts with hypertension indicate an intrinsic (glomerular) cause — investigate for glomerulonephritis/vasculitis.

signs__RENAL / UROLOGICAL__Oliguria / An.question: After confirming pre-renal AKI, besides giving fluids, what is an essential step?
signs__RENAL / UROLOGICAL__Oliguria / An.explanation: Stopping nephrotoxins (NSAIDs, ACEi/ARB, etc.) is essential alongside restoring perfusion in pre-renal AKI.
